outline.description: Sets out the factual backdrop of the domestic‑violence call, the officers’ interaction with Lisa Coleman, the entry into the home, the subsequent investigation leading to a search warrant, and the procedural journey from district court denial of suppression to appeal.
subtopics: 911 emergency call reporting threatened homicide by Jaison Coleman
Officer Kizer’s arrival at the Coleman residence and initial knock‑knock exchange
Lisa’s hesitant responses, denial then eventual agreement to let officers enter
Body‑camera record of the dialogue establishing consent language (“need” to come inside)
Police sweep of the home: locating children, locating Jaison Coleman, protective pat‑down
Obtaining an arrest warrant based on information gleaned after entry
Discovery of multiple firearms during the warrant‑authorized search
Federal indictment for unlawful firearm possession under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1)
District court suppression hearing outcome and Coleman’s guilty plea while preserving appeal
"Procedural timeline" from magistrate’s report through Seventh Circuit review

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2 – The Fourth Amendment Consent Doctrine
outline.description: Explains the legal framework governing consent searches of homes, including third‑party authority, voluntariness requirements, scope analysis, and appellate review standards that govern this case.
subtopics: Consent as an established exception to the Fourth Amendment warrant requirement
"Schneckloth v. Bustamonte" – statutory basis for voluntary consent
"Matlock" & "Cellitti" – when a third party may validly give consent
"Bumper v. North Carolina" – voluntariness must be free from coercion
"United States v. Jones" – totality‑of‑the‑circumstances test for voluntariness
Six‑factor checklist from "Figueroa‑Espana" (age/education, rights advisement, detention length, immediacy vs repeated requests, physical coercion, custody status)
"Jimeno v. United States" – objective reasonableness test for scope of consent
"Saucedo" – limits on what activities fall within granted permission
Standard of appellate review for district‑court findings on consent: clear error

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3 – Voluntariness Analysis in United States v. Coleman
outline.description: Applies the voluntariness standards to Lisa's alleged consent, evaluating officer conduct, her ability to refuse entry, and how the totality-of‑circumstances factors weighed in the Seventh Circuit’s reasoning.
subtopics: Assessment of Lisa’s authority over the premises as co‑habitant spouse/partner
"Initial refusal" (“I’d prefer you not”) demonstrating capacity to deny consent
"Use of ‘need’ language" – how urgency was conveyed without intimidation
"Absence of custody" – Lisa was free to leave at any time
"Length of interaction" – brief exchange lasting only minutes
"Presence/absence of physical coercion or threats" – officer calm demeanor per video record
"Totality‑of‑circumstances factors applied": age/adult status; no advisement required; no prolonged detention; immediate request followed by later voluntary assent; no overt pressure
"Precedent comparison" with "United States v. Hicks", "United States v. Han", "United States v. Figueroa‑Espana" illustrating consistent application
"Court’s conclusion": No clear error in finding Lisa’s consent was freely given

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4 – Scope of Consent and Objective Reasonableness
outline.'description': 'Analyzes whether the officers’ actions after entry exceeded what a reasonably informed homeowner would have authorized under the circumstances described.'
'subtopics': "Objective reasonableness standard" from "Jimeno" applied to this fact pattern
"Officers’ stated purpose": securing safety of children and determining if an armed threat remained present
"Whole‑house sweep": locating occupants and assessing danger as within permissible scope under "Saucedo"
"Protective pat‑down": limited frisk based on articulable safety concerns consistent with initial permission
"Questioning children about gun threats": investigative step tied directly to protecting minors rather than general evidence gathering
"Absence of explicit limitation" expressed by Lisa regarding areas off‑limits or activities prohibited
"Comparison with cases where courts found overreaching", e.g., when officers search unrelated areas or conduct unrelated investigations after entry
"Court’s reasoning": typical reasonable person would infer permission for a thorough visual inspection when officer expressed need for child safety

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 5 – Holding, Rationale, and Broader Significance
outline.description: Summarizes the Seventh Circuit’s decision affirming the district court's denial of suppression, outlines its legal reasoning and discusses implications for future domestic‑violence calls and third‑party consent jurisprudence.
subtopics: "Affirmation" – district court findings on valid consent and proper scope upheld;
"Clear error review": why appellate deference was appropriate given undisputed video record;
"Rejection of alternative doctrines": exigent circumstances & inevitable discovery not needed because consent sufficed;
"Practical guidance for law enforcement": emphasizing respectful request for entry rather than reliance on coercive tactics;
"Impact on third‑party consent cases": reaffirming that spouses/partners can validly authorize entries when they possess common authority;
"Policy considerations": balancing victim safety in domestic‑violence situations against Fourth Amendment privacy interests;
"Future citation value": likely precedent for courts assessing voluntary nature of consent where officers invoke concern for children
